### Prompt 230 — Package the Outlook add-in into a Windows installer, add a C7NC section, and build the O365 app-registration script
**Timestamp:** 2026-10-07 | **Status:** ✅ Completed | **Duration:** ~3 h
**BuildNotes IDs:** 2026.10.7.031 - The Outlook add-in becomes installable: a generated manifest, a Windows installer, and a C7NC section

> Package the email to ticket add-in/plugin for Outlook into a windows installer. Install and configure any tools necessary to accomplish this. Also add a link/button to install it directly from C7NTAX. Place it in a new parent section on the left nav pane named C7NC.
>
> Create a plan/script that will create the Oauth app necessary to enable the Office 365 connector to work. Build it out for me if you can and place it in a folder called O365 along with the instructions

**What I did**
- **Found the blocker before building anything to install.** `apps/outlook-addin/manifest.xml` carries `__ADDIN_HOST__` and `__ADDIN_GUID__`, the README said to replace them by hand, and the API served the file through `express.static` — so `GET /addin/manifest.xml` returned the placeholders. Office refuses a manifest without absolute URLs and reports that by *not showing the add-in*, so the documented install path could never have worked and would have failed silently. Grepping for the placeholder confirmed nothing anywhere substituted it.
- **Made the manifest generated, not static.** `services/addinPackage.ts` renders it for `PUBLIC_BASE_URL` (or the request's own host) with a fixed default identity, and `routes/addin.ts` intercepts `/addin/manifest.xml` before the static handler. One definition, three callers — the served manifest, the installer build, the deployment report. The add-in id is **fixed rather than generated**, because Office treats a new GUID as a different add-in and regenerating one would strand existing sideloads.
- **Installed the toolchain and found a licensing trap.** WiX 7 installed cleanly and then refused to build: it requires accepting the fee-bearing Open Source Maintenance Fee EULA. That is the business's decision, not a build script's, so I moved to **WiX 5.0.2**, which predates the fee, and pinned `5.*` in the script with the reason written down.
- **Proved the mechanism before building the real thing.** A throwaway MSI established that `Scope="perUser"` installs to `%LOCALAPPDATA%` and writes `HKCU` as `REG_SZ`, and that uninstall removes file, value and folder — then the real installer did the same with the real manifest.
- **Hit the MSI version ceiling.** Windows Installer requires `major < 256`, so `2026.10.7` cannot be a package version; WiX warned that the behaviour was undefined. Mapped it to `YY.M.PPPP` — `2026.10.7.031` → `26.10.7031` — which keeps every field in range and the order monotonic, and kept the true version in `build.json`, the filename and the UI.
- **Made the build read the manifest from the server.** `build.ps1` fetches `GET {ApiUrl}/addin/manifest.xml` rather than substituting placeholders itself, so the installer and the hand-downloaded manifest cannot disagree about origin or identity. Parsed the manifest textually: its default XML namespace defeats an unprefixed `SelectSingleNode`.
- **Replaced a HEAD probe with a JSON descriptor.** The page originally decided whether an installer existed from a `HEAD` status. A transient failure would have made it assert that no installer exists — a false claim about a file sitting right there — so `/addin/installer` now returns a description instead, and the page can be wrong about *when*, never about *whether*.
- **Built the C7NC section.** New top-level nav parent with an Outlook Add-in page at `/c7nc/outlook-addin`, routes, header and section-landing descriptions. It offers the installer, the manifest, a manual sideload and centralized deployment, and shows an administrator the served origin, the add-in identity, and the installer's build record — **warning with the rebuild command when the installer was built for a different server**. No permission: it degrades to one explanatory card on a 403 rather than failing, because a technician who cannot read deployment detail should still be able to install the add-in.
- **Caught myself breaking a nav entry and fixed it immediately.** An early edit removed the `help-home` child while inserting the C7NC node; reading the region back showed it and it was restored.
- **Fixed a rebuild that could not reach anyone.** The service worker cached `/addin/*` cache-first, so a rebuilt installer would have come back out of a cache. `/addin/` is now bypassed exactly as `/api/` is, and the cache name is bumped. Added `/addin` to the Vite proxy so the download resolves same-origin in development.
- **Wrote `O365/New-C7NTAXMailboxApp.ps1`** — PLAN-017 §4/§5 as Graph REST instead of portal clicks: device-code sign-in with Microsoft's own Graph CLI client (no module, no `az`), create-or-reuse the registration, request `Mail.ReadWrite` application and/or the delegated scopes, create the service principal, grant admin consent by app-role assignment and `oauth2PermissionsGrants`, create the secret once into a git-ignored file, and **print** the Exchange Online RBAC scoping commands rather than running them.
- **Was honest about what could not be tested.** The script was parse-checked and run against a deliberately nonexistent tenant, which proves the request it builds is well-formed — Microsoft answers `AADSTS90002: Tenant not found` rather than rejecting the call. Everything past the device-code step needs a live tenant and an administrator, so it is documented as not yet executed rather than presented as working.
- **Updated the records.** PLAN-022 (design, thirteen decisions including two rejections, what is left), the plan registry, `installer/README.md`, `O365/README.md`, `apps/outlook-addin/README.md` (which still documented the broken manual-replace path), the Help walkthrough and FAQ, BuildNotes 2026.10.7.031, and the generated fallbacks.

**Decisions worth remembering**
- **Documentation that describes a step the product does not do is a bug report about the product.** The README's "replace the placeholders" was accurate about the file and wrong about the server — and because the server served that same file, following the instructions produced exactly the failure the instructions were meant to prevent.
- **Measure the thing before installing a tool to fix it.** The installer was the request; the manifest was the blocker. Building the MSI first would have produced a perfectly good package that registered a manifest Office cannot load.
- **Ask the server for the truth once, then distribute it.** Fetching the resolved manifest at build time costs the installer its portability and buys a guarantee that the installer, the hand-downloaded manifest and the report cannot disagree. The cost is paid openly: the application compares the origins and says so when they differ.
- **A transient probe is not evidence.** `HEAD` → status would have let the page state something false about a file that exists. Describing the artifact once is strictly more information for no more work.
- **Never accept a licence on the user's behalf.** WiX 6+ gates its build behind a fee. Downgrading to a version that does not is the choice a build script is allowed to make; accepting the fee is not.
- **Per-user is a constraint, not a preference.** The registration is in the signed-in user's hive, so a machine-wide MSI would write a hive Office is not reading and work only for whoever ran it. That single fact decides the install scope, rules out a SYSTEM push, and is why the silent-install command says to run it as the user.
- **A binary cannot tell you what is inside it.** An MSI cannot be inspected for the origin or version baked into it, so `build.json` travels beside it and the deployment report reads that. Without it the mismatch warning would be impossible.

**Notes for next time**
- **WiX 5 builds, WiX 6/7 refuse without accepting the OSMF fee.** `dotnet tool install --global wix --version '5.*'`. The `.wxs` uses the v4 schema (`Scope="perUser"`, `RegistryValue Root="HKCU"`), which 5 accepts unchanged.
- **An MSI package version cannot be `2026.10.7`.** Map the BuildNotes version with `YY.M.PPPP`, or WiX emits `WIX1148` and the ordering guarantee that `MajorUpgrade` depends on is undefined.
- **The installed manifest is the only one that matters.** `%LOCALAPPDATA%\C7NTAX\OutlookAddIn\manifest.xml` after install should contain zero occurrences of `__ADDIN_` — the quickest way to tell a real registration from a stale one.
- **`Stop-Process -Id` needs a literal PID** in this environment: read the PID with `Get-NetTCPConnection … -eq 4000` first, then kill it in a separate call. The array-variable form is rejected by the guard.
- **The installer is built for one origin and says so.** After the production hostname exists (PLAN-016), rebuild with `pwsh -File ./build.ps1 -ApiUrl https://<host>` and commit the new artifact, or the C7NC page will keep showing the rebuild warning.
- **`O365/` is untested past sign-in.** Run it with `-WhatIf` first against a real tenant; the first real run is the test.


### Prompt 231 — A ticket-creation flow for one or many selected emails (mockup first)
**Timestamp:** 2026-10-07 | **Status:** ✅ Completed (mockup; implementation not started) | **Duration:** ~1.5 h
**BuildNotes IDs:** 2026.10.7.032 - The add-in endpoint was dead, and a mockup for the flow that replaces it

> For the Outlook add-in, if multiple e-mails are selected a dialog should pop up and ask whether individual tickets should be created or should they be packaged into a single ticket as attachments. If bundled you should be able to select which one will be the submitted as the aprent ticket and what other ones who be included as attachments. Also There should be a popup asking if you want to see a preview of what the ticket submission will look like to review what fields will be populated in the ticket from the info in the email. You should have the option to edit the info before submitting.
>
> Do a mockup first. Include a simulation of when a single email is selected as well as multiple emails. It should be clean, streamlined, and intuitive.

**What I did**
- **Read the real endpoint before drawing anything**, because a preview screen is a promise about which fields get filled in — and the answer had to be the actual server's, not a guess. That read turned up the bug below.
- **Found `POST /api/outlook-addin/tickets` returning 404 for every request.** `routes/outlookAddin.ts` still gated on `configFlag("integrations", "outlookAddin")` after the field moved to `apps` in 2026.10.7.030. `configValue` answers `""` for an undeclared field, `configFlag` reads that as `false`, so the gate failed **closed**: the taskpane served, every screen reported the feature as on, and the only thing that could create a ticket was unreachable. Proved it live — `404 {"error":"Outlook add-in disabled"}` — then fixed it and proved it again: `201`, one ticket, `MSP-1001-1001`.
- **Swept all 43 config read sites rather than fixing the one I had tripped over**, because a stale area fails silently and this class of drift had just cost a whole feature. Wrote the sweep as `scripts/check-config-reads.mts` (`pnpm guard:config`) and made it read the **real registry** instead of restating it — which is why it runs through `tsx`; `packages/shared` is TypeScript source with extensionless imports and plain `node` cannot load it. It reported exactly one stale read, so the fix was complete rather than merely sufficient, and it names the area a missing field has actually moved to.
- **Built `docs/mockups/outlook-addin-ticket-flow.html`** — a single self-contained file, no build step and no API calls, with a simulation rail (1 / 3 / 5 selected messages, Outlook light or dark) and the pane rendered at its real 360px inside a suggestion of Outlook's chrome.
- **Several messages get the bundle question as a sheet, not a modal window.** Office owns modal dialogs, so a taskpane that opens one fights its own host. Each option states its outcome in tickets — "2 tickets, one per message" versus "A single ticket" — and the flow does not advance until the user has actually chosen.
- **Bundling is two independent decisions**, so it is two controls: which message becomes the ticket (labelled *The ticket*, not left to a radio dot), and which of the others ride along. A message that already has a ticket cannot be the parent and is not offered as an attachment either.
- **The preview is a question, not a step.** A sheet asks whether to review, and "Create now" stays one click away — the review should never become a tax on filing the same kind of ticket all day.
- **The review shows every field as a field**, editable: board, client, contact, subject, description, priority, and a read-only Source. Matched senders say so in green; unmatched ones say so in amber with the picker right there. Several tickets collapse to summary rows with one open at a time, because five forms do not fit in 360px and do not need to.
- **The result is per message**, since "3 created" does not tell somebody which of their messages was already done — each row leads with its ticket number, and skipped rows carry the reason.
- **Added per-screen design notes** to the mockup so the reasoning travels with the artifact and can be reviewed screen by screen, with a toggle to hide them.
- **Driven in the browser through every path**, then the copy bugs fixed: a footer that counted an already-ticketed message as an attachment (2 when only 1 could ride along), "1 messages", "from the messages" for a single message, and Back from an individual-ticket preview that went to a bundling step the user had never seen.

**Decisions worth remembering**
- **Ask the server before designing the screen that describes it.** The preview exists to show which fields the server fills in; designing it from imagination would have produced a screen that lies about the payload. Reading the handler is what surfaced a dead endpoint.
- **Moving a config field is a breaking change with no compile error.** The registry is typed, the read is a string pair, and `configValue` returns `""` for anything it cannot find — so the failure is a feature that is off while every screen says it is on. That is the third distinct silent-failure mode in this area (the others were a module-scope read and a cached cross-origin 404), and it is now the only one with a guard.
- **A guard is worth writing when the failure is silent and the check is mechanical.** One stale read out of 43 is exactly the case: cheap to check, impossible to notice, and the cost of missing it is a feature nobody can use.
- **The bundle question is asked, never guessed.** Three messages can be three unrelated problems or one incident, and only the user knows which. Defaulting either way encodes a wrong assumption into a habit.
- **"One ticket each" and "the rest attached" are not symmetric choices**, so the option copy leads with the consequence — a count of tickets — rather than with the mechanism.
- **Bundling is two axes, so it is two controls.** Collapsing "which is the parent" and "which ride along" into one picker would force all-or-nothing and make the parent choice carry a meaning it does not have.
- **One field set for one ticket and for five.** The same review for both means one shape to learn, and it keeps bundled and individual from feeling like two different products.
- **Stating the arithmetic before the user commits** — "1 message already has a ticket and will be skipped, so 2 tickets will be created" — is what stops a half-working outcome from looking like a bug at the end.

**Notes for next time**
- **`pnpm guard:config` exists now.** Run it after any change to `packages/shared/src/appConfiguration.ts`. It catches a moved or renamed field, which is otherwise invisible.
- **A `configFlag("area", "field")` pair where the field has moved fails closed and silently.** If a feature is switched on in the UI but its endpoint 404s, check the area before anything else.
- **The mockup is not wired in and nothing references it.** It lives at `docs/mockups/outlook-addin-ticket-flow.html`; open it directly in a browser.
- **The flow is not implemented.** The endpoint today still takes `{ boardId, emails[] }` and creates one ticket per message — bundling, the preview and per-field edits all need server work (`createTicketFromEmail` currently ignores whatever the pane sends beyond the message fields, and note the endpoint tests the flag in `integrations`, now fixed).
- **The mockup's field set is the contract for the server change**: board, client, contact, subject, description, priority, plus attachments and a parent for bundled mode. Whoever implements it should change the endpoint to accept the reviewed fields rather than re-deriving them.
- **A layout check beats a screenshot for mockups**: measuring `scrollWidth` against `clientWidth` for the pane and every descendant caught nothing, but it is the check that would have found an overflowing row in a 360px pane — the failure mode a narrow taskpane is most prone to.


### Prompt 232 — Saved preferences in the add-in mockup, so a selection can be one click
**Timestamp:** 2026-10-07 | **Status:** ✅ Completed (mockup) | **Duration:** ~40 min
**BuildNotes IDs:** 2026.10.7.033 - Save my preferences: the add-in flow can stop asking

> Add a save my preferences option to the mockup, so that it will allow single click creation in the future.

**What I did**
- **Added saved preferences to the mockup**, held in `localStorage` so they survive a reload and belong to the mailbox rather than to the browser session. Three answers: how several messages are handled (*ask* or *one ticket per message*), whether the review is offered (*ask*, *always*, or **never — create immediately**), and whether the last board used is remembered.
- **Put "Remember this answer" on the questions themselves**, so a preference is set where it is decided rather than by first finding a settings page. On the preview question it means **whichever button is pressed** — remember "create without asking", or remember "always show me first" — because the answer is the answer either way.
- **Made the entry screen say what the preferences will do before the button acts on them.** With both answers saved the label becomes **Create 2 tickets now**, the note underneath reads "2 tickets filed immediately — no questions, per your saved preferences", and an **One-click** chip marks the state. A preference that changes behaviour silently is how somebody files something they did not mean to.
- **Added a Preferences screen reachable from a ⚙ in the pane header and from the entry screen.** This is the part that matters most: every one of these preferences works by making a question *stop appearing*, so once it has taken effect this screen is the only evidence it was ever set. It states the consequence in prose for the current combination — including the one case that files tickets with nothing shown first — keeps *Ask each time* as a first-class option rather than a hidden default, and has a **Reset**.
- **Refused to make bundling rememberable, and said so in the sheet.** Which message is the ticket changes per conversation, so "always bundle" would have to invent a parent. The remember checkbox appears for *One ticket each* and is replaced by that explanation for *One ticket, the rest attached* — an honest gap beats a checkbox that guesses.
- **Added "New selection (keeps preferences)" to the rail**, because that is the demonstration: the selection changes, the preferences do not, and the same button takes a different path. "Reset flow & clear preferences" is the way back to a first run, and the rail's Preferences row shows *asking*, *saved* or *one-click* at a glance.
- **Found and fixed a layout defect by measuring.** Rows in the picker lists overflowed the 360px pane: `text-overflow: ellipsis` does not apply to an inline box, and those rows are built from `<span>`s while the message rows are built from `<div>`s. `msg-who` and `msg-sub` are now `display: block` so the ellipsis works whichever tag builds the row.

**Decisions worth remembering**
- **A preference that silences a question has to be visible in three places**: where it is set (the checkbox on the question), where it takes effect (the notice and chip on the entry screen), and in one place it can be undone (the Preferences screen). Without all three, the third is a treasure hunt and the first two look like the product behaving unpredictably.
- **"Never ask" is offered, and named honestly.** Its sub-label says the ticket is filed as soon as you press Create rather than dressing it up as "streamline the process". A confirm-free path is a real thing to want and a real thing to be told you are choosing.
- **Some questions should not be rememberable.** Remembering "one ticket per message" removes a question with one right answer for that person; remembering "bundle" would remove a question about which message is the ticket, which has no default. An honest gap in the settings beats a guess made on the user's behalf.
- **"Remember this answer" is better than a pre-selection.** The flow still asks the first time, still shows both outcomes, and only stops asking once the user has actually answered — so nothing is decided for somebody who has never seen the choice.
- **Measuring catches what looking does not.** The ellipsis defect was invisible in a snapshot (the text was clipped in the source, not on screen) and obvious to arithmetic on `clientWidth` versus `scrollWidth`.
- **Preferences are device-scoped, not account-scoped, in the mockup.** That is the honest default for an add-in — the pane is the user's own Outlook — and it avoids implying a server-side preference store that does not exist.

**Notes for next time**
- **Preferences are in `localStorage` under `c7ntax.addin.mockup.prefs`.** Clearing it resets a first run; the rail's "Reset flow & clear preferences" does the same from inside the mockup.
- **The implementation still needs somewhere to keep these.** A per-user preference is a `User` column or a settings row, and the pane needs it at sign-in — that is a server change, so it belongs in the same work as the flow itself.
- **The flow and the preferences remain unimplemented.** The mockup is the design of record for both; `docs/mockups/outlook-addin-ticket-flow.html` is the only artifact.
- **The overflow check is worth keeping as a habit for any narrow-surface work.** It is four lines in the browser console and it found a defect that three rounds of reading the CSS had not.


### Prompt 233 — Implement the add-in flow, version the plugin, and keep every installer
**Timestamp:** 2026-10-07 | **Status:** ✅ Completed | **Duration:** ~3 h
**BuildNotes IDs:** 2026.10.7.034 - The add-in flow ships, the plugin gets a version, and every installer is kept; 2026.10.7.035 - A picked client no longer swallows the contact, and the flow is under test

> Looks great. Implment it. update the plugin and installer as well. Going forward if changes are made to the plugin, the installer should be updated too.
>
> Create a list of past versions of the installer in the Outlook Add-in page (see screenshot), so that previous versions can be downloaded and installed for troubleshooting purposes or last known good config. Apply a version numbering system to the plugin

**What I did**
- **Built the flow that the mockup specified, in the pane and on the server.** Several selected messages ask *one ticket each* or *one ticket with the others attached*; bundling asks which message is the parent; the preview sheet offers the review; the review shows every field the server will fill in — board, client, contact, subject, description, priority — and all of them are editable before submitting.
- **Added `POST /api/outlook-addin/preview` so the review is real rather than decorative.** The client is matched from the sender's domain and the contact from the sender's address, and the pane can see neither. The server is asked what it *would* do, read-only, and reports which messages already have a ticket, so the pane shows that on the row instead of it being discovered at the end.
- **Added `GET /api/outlook-addin/options`** so the pane can offer boards and clients without demanding the permissions `/api/boards` and `/api/clients` enforce. Filing a ticket does not require `ClientView`, and a technician who could create a ticket but not list clients was being shown an empty picker.
- **Bundled messages ride along as `.eml` attachments** — headers plus the plain-text body, so the original can be opened later rather than read as a re-rendered summary. Whole-message attachments are size-checked and deliberately non-fatal: the ticket exists, and failing the whole submission because one message was too large would report failure for work that was done.
- **Reviewed fields win over deduction.** A chosen client, a corrected contact name, an edited subject, description or priority are applied rather than re-derived. The contact rename is real — an editable field that quietly does nothing is worse than one that is not offered — and it is logged.
- **Moved saved preferences onto the `User` row** (`addinPreferences`) rather than the pane's `localStorage`, which is scoped to the add-in's origin and therefore shared by every C7NTAX account used on that machine. *Remember this answer* sits on both questions; the **Preferences** screen is the one place a saved answer is seen and undone, because every one of them works by making a question stop appearing. Verified end to end that with both saved a later selection files **with no sheet shown at all**; bundling is deliberately not rememberable and the sheet says why.
- **Gave the plugin a version.** `apps/outlook-addin/plugin.json` records its identity, its `YY.M.PPPP` version derived from the release, and a hash of the files that make it up (`packages/shared/src/addinPlugin.ts`, SHA-256 over a length-prefixed, path-qualified payload list). The manifest's `<Version>` is served from the same record, so the version Office reports, the MSI filename and the install page cannot disagree. The add-in's GUID moved into that record with it.
- **Made "if the plugin changes, the installer must be updated" enforced rather than remembered.** `pnpm guard:plugin` fails on a payload change with no version bump, a version mismatch, or a missing installer, and `build.ps1` refuses outright rather than producing an installer for an unversioned plugin. Proved both on a real change before trusting them.
- **Replaced the single `build.json` with a release history** (`installer/artifacts/index.json`): version, release, origin, payload hash, build time and SHA-256 per artifact, newest first, with a rebuild of the same version replacing its entry rather than adding a second. The API serves **only** names in that history, so a download path can never become a filesystem path.
- **Added the Installer versions card to C7NC → Outlook Add-in** — every version with its own Download, the current one labelled **Newest**, an entry built from different files marked **Older plugin files**, and a stale banner naming the rebuild command when the newest installer does not match the plugin being served.
- **Found and fixed a second real bug by driving the pane in a browser:** every write returned `403 CSRF token missing or invalid` while every read worked. `fetch` sends the origin's cookies by default, so with a valid C7NTAX session cookie present the API demanded a CSRF header despite the bearer token. The pane is a token client, so it now sends `credentials: "omit"`. Also corrected a hint that told the user the wrong thing about the unmatched-client case.
- **Found a third bug by extending the add-in's own probe: choosing a client in the review skipped contact creation, so the contact name the user had just confirmed was dropped.** The probe section for the reviewed fields failed on its rename assertion, which looked like a probe assumption and turned out to be a behaviour: when the review supplies a client, sender resolution returned that client and stopped, and the contact lookup on that path was lookup-only — so for a sender with no contact yet the ticket was filed against **no contact at all**. A picked client now wins over *matching* rather than over the rest of resolution: the contact is created under the chosen client and the reviewed name is applied to it. Fixed in `resolveSender`, and the probe grew from 32 checks to **59** covering `/options`, `/preview`, the reviewed fields, the bundled ticket and per-user preferences.

**Decisions worth remembering**
- **A guard is only worth having if you have watched it fail.** Both the plugin guard and the build were run against a genuine unversioned change first; a check that has only ever passed is indistinguishable from a check that does nothing.
- **One plugin version per application release.** The version is derived from the release at the top of BuildNotes, so a payload change inside a release must advance the release. Deriving it means it is never typed and never wrong.
- **The plugin's identity is not part of its version.** The GUID is fixed and lives in the record; a regenerated GUID is a different add-in and would strand every mailbox that had already sideloaded.
- **`plugin.json` is not in the payload hash**, or bumping the record would change the hash it holds.
- **A history is not a single build record with more fields.** One record can only describe one build: the previous installer would have been overwritten with no way to say which version it had been, and the rollback the user asked for would have had nothing to point at.
- **Saved preferences belong to the person, not to the machine.** The pane's `localStorage` is shared by every account used on that PC, and a preference that lets a ticket be filed without asking, inherited by the next person to use Outlook, is not a preference.
- **The review has to be able to change the outcome, or it is decoration.** Hence read-only preview on the server, and reviewed values applied in preference to deduction.

**Notes for next time**
- **Keep the three CI guards green together:** `guard:config` (43 reads, all declared), `guard:plugin`, `guard:routes` (393/347/0), plus `check-help-links.mjs` (75 routes / 20 walkthroughs / 44 links). The add-in's own probe is the fourth regression gate, and the one that found the contact defect — extend it whenever the flow changes.
- **A probe assertion that fails is a question, not an obstacle.** "and renamed the contact it will be filed against" failed as `undefined undefined`, which was one grep away from a genuine defect. Read the failure before relaxing the check.
- **A payload change now needs both steps:** `pnpm plugin:bump` then `pnpm installer:build`. Building without the bump is refused rather than silently producing a mislabelled MSI. A server-side change that does not touch the plugin needs neither — the guard compares the plugin against its installer, not against the release.
- **Diagnose the add-in in the browser, not by reading the code.** Real Office.js overwrites a stubbed `window.Office` and switches the pane back off; block `**/appsforoffice.microsoft.com/**` and cache-bust `**/addin/taskpane.*`, and the whole flow is drivable without Outlook.
- **Both "empty pane" causes are now reported rather than guessed at** — an installer built for another origin, and an installer built before the current plugin files. Both appear on the C7NC page with the command that fixes them.
- **The probe leaves nothing behind:** tickets, attachment rows, the `.eml` files those rows point at, the contacts it created, and the sessions it signed in with are all removed, and it restores the admin's preferences to defaults.


### Prompt 234 — The add-in says "bundle", and a simulator so it can be seen without installing it
**Timestamp:** 2026-10-07 | **Status:** ✅ Completed | **Duration:** ~1 h 45 min
**BuildNotes IDs:** 2026.10.7.036 - The add-in says "bundle", and can be tried without installing it

> In the plug-in change "with gaps" to something easier to understand like "bundled" to better make sense of what the intended purpose is. Update the verbiage to explain better. This is user facing, so it should be simple, intuitive, and easy to understand.
>
> On the Outlook Add-in Configuration page under Administration, create an option/button to launch a pop-up window that will simulate the plug-in in action. I want to be able to see and interact with a demo of the plugin without haiving to install it. Kind of like how DummyConnect works. It won't actually do anything, but you can simulate the submission scenarios from start to finish.

**What I did**
- **Renamed the choice, not just the label.** "One ticket, the rest attached" described the mechanism — what happens to the *other* messages — without saying what the choice is, so the reader had to work out that "bundle" was the word they wanted. It is now **Bundle into one ticket**, and the whole path says bundle: the preferences screen, the saved-answers notice, the result line, the help walkthrough and the FAQ.
- **Rewrote the option copy to lead with the outcome**: *All 3 messages become a single ticket. You choose which one the ticket is written from; the other 2 are attached to it as files you can open later.* The question above it became **"Which message should the ticket be written from?"**, because a ticket is written *from* a message rather than being one.
- **Read the rest of the flow's copy as a reader for the first time.** "Attached messages ride along as .eml attachments on the one ticket" became *"Each attached message is saved on the ticket as a file, so anyone reading it later can open the original"*; the entry screen's promise for several messages became *"You'll choose one ticket each or bundled, then whether to review"* instead of "you'll be asked how to handle them". The mockup was updated in step, since it is the design of record.
- **Found the phrase the user was quoting** — "Multiple, with gaps" was a simulation-scenario name in the mockup, describing five messages of which two match no client, and the rail now says **"Several emails, two unmatched"** with the scenario explained in a sentence instead of a fragment.
- **Built the simulator as the shipped pane rather than a copy of it.** `GET /addin/taskpane.html?demo=1` runs the real taskpane: `api()` is answered by `demoAnswer()` with canned boards, clients, a shaped-like-the-server preview and fabricated ticket numbers, so every screen, question and result is the one the add-in uses. A second interface written to look like the first drifts the moment the flow changes, and a demo that shows something the add-in does not do is worse than no demo.
- **Gave it three selections and a way back to the start**, chosen to cover the paths worth seeing: one email, three (one already ticketed), and five with two senders matching no client — the case the preview exists for. The strip at the top says plainly that nothing is created, sent or saved.
- **Offered it where the add-in is switched on**, per the request: **Administration → Configuration → Client Apps & Notifications → Open the simulator** opens it in a window sized like the pane. It is a pop-up rather than an inline panel because the pane is 360px wide and designed to sit beside a mailbox — inline it would demonstrate a layout the add-in does not have.
- **Gated the button on the setting that serves it.** The simulator lives on the add-in's own endpoint, so with the add-in off the button is disabled and says why, rather than opening a page that answers 404.
- **Let the guard do its job.** Changing the pane is a change to the plugin, so `pnpm guard:plugin` failed and named both problems (the payload hash had drifted and the newest installer was built from the old payload) — which is the enforcement asked for in the previous prompt working on the very next change. `pnpm plugin:bump` then `pnpm installer:build` took it to 26.10.7036, with the previous two installers still downloadable.

**Decisions worth remembering**
- **Rename the choice, not the button.** "The rest attached" and "bundle" are the same mechanism described from two ends; the one that names the *outcome* is the one a person can decide on. Wherever the flow refers to the choice it now says bundle, because two names for one thing is how a flow starts to feel like two flows.
- **A demo built from the product cannot drift from the product.** The alternative — a nice standalone mockup page — would have been quicker and would have started lying the first time the flow changed. The mockup already exists for design; the simulator exists to be true.
- **Canned answers must mirror the real response shape.** The pane reads `matchedCompany`, `fallbackCompany`, `contactName`, `title`, `description` and `priority`; a demo that invented its own shape would demonstrate a flow the add-in does not have.
- **Say what is not real, on the screen where it is not real.** "Simulator — the real add-in pane, with example messages. Nothing is created, sent or saved." sits above everything else, and the result rows carry an **Example** chip instead of an **Open** link that would go nowhere.
- **Gate a demo on the thing that serves it.** A button that opens a 404 is worse than a button that explains it cannot open yet.

**Notes for next time**
- **`?demo=1` is part of the plugin's payload**, so a change to the simulator moves the plugin version and requires an installer rebuild. That is correct — it is a change to the files the add-in runs — but it is worth knowing before wondering why the guard fired.
- **The simulation scenario names live in two places on purpose**: the mockup's rail (`Several emails, two unmatched`) and the pane's strip (`Five, two unmatched`). The mockup is written for a reviewer, the pane for somebody clicking.
- **`window.open` cannot be exercised through the browser tooling here** — popups are blocked for programmatic clicks and the app's animated containers make Playwright's stability check time out. Verified instead by stubbing `window.open` and dispatching the button's own click handler, which confirmed the handler fires with `/addin/taskpane.html?demo=1`, plus loading that URL directly on both origins.


### Prompt 235 — A full bug and security audit, the advisory re-run, and the fixes that were safe to make
**Timestamp:** 2026-10-07 | **Status:** ✅ Completed | **Duration:** ~2 h 30 min
**BuildNotes IDs:** 2026.10.7.037 - A full security and bug audit: five holes closed, and the ones left are named

> Audit the codebase for bugs and fix any you find. Ensure all buttons, links, and other UI elements function as intended, except for the ones that have intentionally not been wired up.
>
> Then run the codebase against the CVE database again and list required updates. Fix any exploits that won't break the app. list out patches any that potentially will break it, but do not fix them yet

**What I did**
- **Audited the whole API surface by running it, not by reading it.** All 28 probes in `apps/api`, plus every guard. Three failed: `probe-billing-batch` (5), `probe-billing-generate-flag` (3) and — in the run where I killed the API mid-suite — most of the rest. Reading their headers first would have saved the detour: both document environment preconditions (`INVOICE_BATCH_ENABLED`, `TIME_RULES_ENABLED`, `EGRESS_ALLOW_PRIVATE`, `BILLING_FROM_TICKETS_ENABLED`). Re-run with them set they pass **36/36 and 6/6**, which is the kill switches working. `probe-expenses` (8 failures, then 27/0) and `probe-kb-autogen` (a stack trace, then 42/0) were casualties of the same restarts. **No product bug came out of the probe suite.**
- **Answered "do the buttons work" with three deterministic checks rather than clicking.** (1) A purpose-written auditor resolves the API's route table through the router mounts and matches it against **every** path the web app requests — 386 routes, 332 calls, **zero broken** (the five it flagged were its own parsing artifacts: `?query` templates, string-concatenated ids, `fetch` prefixes). (2) `guard:routes`: 393 routes / 347 guarded / 0 unguarded. (3) The grep sweep for dead affordances — `onClick={() => {}}`, `href="#"`, `TODO`/`not implemented` — found nothing. The integrated browser disconnected part-way through the route sweep, so per-page clicking was replaced by these; the honest limitation is recorded below.
- **Found the sharpest hole in the audit's first read: `GET /system/config/:key` had no gate.** Its `PATCH` twin did, and the route-guard exemption claimed the route was "guarded per key" — true of one verb, false of the other. The SSO callback parks `sso:oidc_code` there: the single-use code **and the signing-in user's live token**. Anyone signed in could poll that key during somebody's SSO sign-in and take their session, never calling the exchange endpoint that exists to consume the code. Fixed with one policy shared by read and write, service-owned rows refused to everyone including administrators, and the same rows omitted from the `/system/configs` dump.
- **Found the widest: the integration list returned cleartext credentials to a role that cannot manage them.** `IntegrationView` is held by Technicians, `IntegrationManage` is not — so a technician could read the M365 client secret, the ConnectWise key pair and the AWS `secretAccessKey` for the whole provider, and use them through `/:id/test` and `/:id/sync`. The projection withholds `credentials` from a non-manager and reports `hasCredentials`; the manage-gated fix dialog is untouched and now says why it cannot open for a view-only user.
- **Closed the cross-company holes, writes first.** `POST /projects`, `POST /quotes`, `POST /schedule` and the add-in's `POST /tickets` took a company from the request body, reachable by `client_admin`/`client_user` — so a forwarded email was enough to file against another client. The body is now checked against the caller's own company, the add-in pins a scoped account to its own client, and the scope check runs **before** the per-message loop so the pane gets a 403 rather than the per-message handler's "the ticket could not be created" — which would have told the person a plausible story about a broken connection instead of the truth about their permissions.
- **Then the reads:** projects, assets, schedule and quotes (with line-item pricing) had no company filter at all — the `companyId` query parameter was the caller's choice and absent by default. Six endpoints scoped, detail routes answering 404 rather than 403. Same for the knowledge base: `KBView` is held by client roles and the article route ignored `status` and `visibility`, so drafts carrying the review note and the originating ticket were readable by the customer they were written about.
- **Re-ran the advisory database and closed the gap behind the overrides.** 4 advisories, **0 in production**, all already accepted with reasons; the only two with a published fix need a major (Tailwind 4, Electron 35+), so they are listed. Then the finding that mattered: the twelve security overrides live in `package.json`, which pnpm 9.1.0 reads and pnpm 10+ **ignores** — and this machine runs a pnpm 11.20.0 wrapper. Proved it in a scratch project rather than reasoning about it: the same override with no `packageManager` pin did nothing and `qs` fell to 6.11.0. The floors are now in `pnpm-workspace.yaml` as well, and `guard:deps` fails on drift between the two lists.
- **Grew the probes rather than trusting the fixes.** The house rule is that a fix with no assertion is a fix that comes back: `probe-configuration` 87 → 91, `probe-cloudconnect-status` 28 → 34, `probe-scoping` 13 → 26, `probe-outlook-addin` 59 → 63.

**Decisions worth remembering**
- **Two copies of a security control are worse than one, unless the drift is checked.** The overrides existed twice in effect (`package.json` and the lockfile) and the second copy was the only reason they still worked. The parity check is the actual fix; adding the second declaration is just the repair.
- **A shared policy beats a second implementation.** The read gate was missing precisely because the write gate was a private function; `assertConfigAccess(user, key, action)` now serves both, so the next verb cannot inherit one and not the other.
- **Prove the premise in a scratch project.** Two one-line experiments (with and without `packageManager`) settled in a minute what an hour of reasoning about pnpm's release notes would not have.
- **Fix the refusal, not just the outcome.** The add-in's scope check *worked* from the moment I wrote it — it threw inside the per-message try/catch, so the request returned 201 with "the ticket could not be created" and nothing created. Correct outcome, dishonest message. Moved it in front of the loop.
- **Check who holds the permission, not just that one is required.** Both the integration leak and the KB leak were "the route has a permission" — just one that client-facing or view-only roles also hold.
- **A probe that fails may be a probe that needs its environment.** Read the header before debugging the product; three of the five failures were preconditions, and verifying them properly turned into evidence that the kill switches work.

**Notes for next time**
- **The browser tooling disconnected mid-audit**, so the per-page click-through did not happen. What replaced it is stronger for *links and endpoints* (every call path resolved, every route guarded) and weaker for *interaction* — a button wired to a handler that throws at runtime would not have been caught. Re-run the route sweep when the browser is back.
- **Listed, not fixed, with reasons in `PLAN-018` Appendix C:** report colour values reaching an HTML sink unescaped (CSP-dependent, below the reporting bar, belongs with the reporting work); integrations storing credentials in cleartext where `email-connectors` encrypts them (schema change); the remaining company-scoped modules (procurement, contracts, checklists, surveys, CRM opportunities) which need their own assertions to be trustworthy; and the two major upgrades that would clear the last fixable advisories.
- **`pnpm install --lockfile-only` is the cheap way to prove an override edit is inert**: it re-resolved the whole workspace and produced a byte-identical `pnpm-lock.yaml`.
- **Watch for the 15-minute auto-sync**; it commits work before the intended commit message exists.

### Prompt 236 — The Installer Versions card split into a current release and its history (mockup)
**Timestamp:** 2026-10-07 | **Status:** ✅ Completed | **Duration:** ~25 min
**BuildNotes IDs:** 2026.10.7.038 - A mockup of the installer versions card, split between the current release and the history behind it

> I want to separate the latest release from the older versions. Inside the Installer Versions card, the latest release should have it's own card with a title above it labeled Latest Release.
>
> The older versions can be grouped together in a card underneath it with a title labeled Previous Versions.
>
> Keep the main title Installer Versions.
>
> Make the font size of the Latest Release and Older Versions labels smaller, but still clearly defined as a header.
>
> Do a mockup first. Don't make any changes yet

**What I did**
- **Measured the card before drawing it.** The obvious way to build this mockup is from the screenshot; that reliably gets the greys wrong and invents spacing. The five values that matter were read out of the application instead — `--surface #0f1a2e`, `--surface-border #2a3a5c`, `--cyber-400 #26cbf6`, the 14px `text-sm font-medium` main title, and the `Chip` tones — along with the real markup in `OutlookAddIn.tsx`, so the mockup reuses the live stale banner sentence, the real release/size/date line and the real closing note word for word. What is being reviewed is what would ship, at the size it would ship at.
- **Sized the two labels below the card's own title rather than beside it.** 11px, semibold, uppercase, `0.06em` tracking, in the tertiary grey — the size goes down and the weight, capitals and tracking take over the job of reading as a header. At the title's 14px the label competes with it; at 10px or below it reads as metadata. The mockup carries that as a spec block so the number is arguable rather than implied.
- **Gave each group one border instead of one per row.** The rows keep their padding and their chips but stop being individually boxed and are separated by a hairline divider, so they read as members of a group. Boxing a bordered row inside a bordered group card would have shown the seam the grouping exists to remove. The latest group is left un-tinted on purpose: the *Newest* chip and the label above it already say which one is current, and a third signal is noise — the tinted alternative is shown and rejected in the notes.
- **Verified every state the card can be in, not just the one in the screenshot.** The page was rendered in headless Edge and the DOM asserts 3 rows / 2 group cards / both labels, and then all six combinations of before-after and three states were driven programmatically: the everyday case (latest + 2 previous), a single version, and the stale-installer banner. The single-version case is where the grouping changes behaviour, and it is flagged rather than smuggled in.
- **Raised the two questions the regrouping creates instead of deciding them quietly.** With a *Previous Versions* label over the old rows, the *Earlier* chip on each of them says the same thing twice; and because the card is currently hidden unless there are two or more versions, a fresh deployment offers no installer download on this page at all — which the *Latest Release* group no longer justifies. Both are called out in the mockup with a recommendation, and both are behaviour decisions rather than layout ones.

**Decisions worth remembering**
- **Take the tokens from the source, not from the screenshot.** A mockup that is 95% right wastes a review round on colours and spacing instead of on the decision.
- **The card's own title stays.** The request was to group inside it, not to re-title it, so `Installer versions` and its `plugin 26.10.7036` fact are untouched — including the `versions.length > 1` gate, which the mockup deliberately leaves as-is while flagging what it now costs.
- **One border per group, hairline between rows.** Nesting bordered rows inside a bordered card is the most common way this grouping looks worse than the flat list.
- **Show the edge states in the mockup itself, not in the covering note.** The single-version state is the one that changes behaviour, and it is a click away in the same file.

**Notes for next time**
- **Nothing in `apps/web` was touched** and no API was called; the deliverable is `docs/mockups/installer-versions-card.html` (self-contained, no build, no network).
- **The integrated browser is still disconnected** ("No client was connected"), so the mockup was verified by rendering it in headless Edge and asserting the DOM rather than by clicking it — the same substitution the previous prompt had to make. Screenshots can be produced with `msedge --headless=new --screenshot`.
- **Implementation is blocked on approval by the request itself.** When it lands it is a small change to the one card in `OutlookAddIn.tsx`, plus the two open questions above.

### Prompt 237 — The regrouped installer versions card, built
**Timestamp:** 2026-10-07 | **Status:** ✅ Completed | **Duration:** ~40 min
**BuildNotes IDs:** 2026.10.7.039 - The installer versions card leads with the release in use, and keeps the rest beneath it

> build it

**What I did**
- **Built the approved mockup in the card it was drawn from.** `VersionRow` carries a row's chips, meta and Download, and the two groups are `Latest Release` and `Previous Versions` with the card's own title and `plugin` fact untouched. Rows are destructured as `const [latest, ...previous] = versions` rather than indexed — with `noUncheckedIndexedAccess` this is the difference between a narrowing the type-checker believes and a `!` it does not.
- **Took the one behaviour change the mockup flagged, and made the one it recommended against a no-op.** The card renders from `latest` rather than `versions.length > 1`, so a deployment with a single installer offers it instead of showing nothing at all; the marketing-free tint on the newest group was left out. The now-redundant *Earlier* chip was kept, because the mockup kept it — the change under review is the grouping, and that stays a one-line follow-up.
- **Caught two classes that silently did nothing, by reading computed styles back out of the running app.** `bg-surface-lighter/40` computed to `rgba(0, 0, 0, 0)` and `divide-surface-border/60` to Tailwind's default `#e5e7eb` — a light-grey hairline in a dark theme. An opacity modifier on a theme colour defined as a bare `var()` emits **no rule**: there is nothing to interpolate the alpha into, so the element falls back to the preflight border colour and nobody sees an error. Replaced with the plain `bg-surface-light` and `divide-surface-border` tokens, then confirmed: panel `rgb(19, 19, 22)`, divider `rgb(42, 42, 49)`, both the theme's own values.
- **Regressed the card against the live page rather than against the diff.** The integrated browser is still down, so I drove headless Edge over the DevTools protocol: signed in through `POST /api/auth/login`, navigated to `/c7nc/outlook-addin`, and asserted the DOM and its computed styles. Result: title 14px/500, labels 11px/600 uppercase 0.66px tracked, 2 group cards, 3 rows, 1 *Newest* / 2 *Earlier* / 2 *Older plugin files*, 3 Downloads with the first pointing at the 26.10.7036 MSI, dividers 0px on the group's first row and 1px on the second, footnote intact, stale banner correctly absent. `probe-outlook-addin` 63/63 — the contract the card reads is unchanged.
- **Updated help where it describes the card**, in both places: the companion-clients FAQ answer on rolling back an add-in update, and the "Installer versions" section of the Outlook Add-in walkthrough. Both now name the two groups rather than describing one list.

**Decisions worth remembering**
- **The mockup was more accurate than the app's own idioms, and that is a warning.** The mockup used `color-mix`, which resolved; the Tailwind opacity modifiers it was *translating from* resolve to nothing. Copying the app's class names is not the same as copying the app's rendering.
- **Read computed styles, not class strings.** `groupClasses` printed the class list and looked perfect; the element was transparent. One `getComputedStyle` per property caught what the class attribute could not.
- **A template-literal label needs its space in the markup.** `Previous Versions{" "}<span>` — JSX strips the trailing whitespace at a line break, so the accessible text read "Previous Versions2 kept" while looking right on screen.
- **Keep the `<p>` labels as `<p>`.** They read as headers and the grouping is visible to a screen reader without adding a heading that is not a section.

**Notes for next time**
- **Reported, not fixed: ~106 opacity modifiers on `bg-*`/`border-*`/`divide-*` surface tokens across 36 files**, where the modifier alone is the only colour source (e.g. `divide-surface-border/60` in `reportKit.tsx` and `PortalTickets.tsx`, `border-b border-surface-border/40` in table rows). They render Tailwind's default grey rather than the theme's border. The real fix is to make the palette tokens alpha-capable — channel triplets (`--surface-border: 42 58 92`) with `rgb(var(--surface-border) / <alpha-value>)` in the Tailwind config — which touches every palette and belongs in its own change with its own verification, not in a card regroup.
- **Vite on this machine is bound to `::1` only**, so `http://127.0.0.1:3010` fails with `000` while `http://localhost:3010` returns 200. The API on 4000 is on IPv4. Worth knowing before blaming the dev server.
- **The one-line follow-up left open:** drop the *Earlier* chip now that the group label says it.

### Prompt 238 — Service Alerts: the 149 notices a stray social sweep put on the board, and the rule that stops them
**Timestamp:** 2026-10-07 | **Status:** ✅ Completed | **Duration:** ~2 h 15 min
**BuildNotes IDs:** 2026.10.7.040 - Service Alerts: a post has to name the service before it can raise a notice

> Fix these errors in the service alerts

**What I did**
- **Read the screenshot as three separate faults and went to the data behind each, rather than fixing the words.** The cards said two things at once: an alert attributed to **X (Twitter)** with "No monitored sources configured" written underneath it, and a divider drawn in a light grey on a dark card. Both were real. The third thing on the card — the title naming one service and the body naming another — turned out to be the symptom of something much larger.
- **Found the cause on the first query: the monitor was reading the probe's stub as X.** `apps/api/probe-outage-board.mjs` points `X_API_BASE_URL` at a local stub that answers *any* search with one canned post, so while the API ran under the probe's environment every service on the board was told the same thing. The count was **149 alerts** — 10 active, 139 auto-resolved — across Microsoft 365, Verizon, Gemini, Claude, AWS, GitHub and the rest, all quoting `ProbeSocial muyrdu93 is down again, nothing loads`. The monitor was behaving exactly as written; nothing in it asked whether the post was about the service it was asking about.
- **Fixed it where it belongs, in the observer.** The recent-search query asks for the service's name, but a search can answer with posts that merely share its words — and a base URL pointed somewhere it should not be answers with anything at all. A post now has to name the service to count for it, so it can neither raise a notice nor retire one, and the detail line says how many of the posts read actually named it (`1 recent post read, 0 naming …`). The positive path is untouched: a post that does name the service still raises the notice, which the probe re-verified.
- **Cleaned the data, including the part that would have restored it.** Deleted the 149 fabricated alerts, the five `ProbeSocial` services that had been left behind, and then recaptured the seed snapshots, because the same rows were sitting in `apps/api/src/snapshots/service-alerts.json` — a reseed would have put the whole thing back. The one genuine alert on the board (a vendor status page reporting a degraded service) was left alone.
- **Repaired the two things on the card that the user could actually see.** The Sources block no longer renders inside an alert when the service's last poll read nothing — it contradicted the source chip on the same card, and the board's Sources column still says when nothing is watching a service, which is that column's whole job. And the divider was `border-surface-border/60`, which emits no CSS at all: the token is a bare `var()`, so there is nothing for the alpha to go into and the element falls back to the preflight border — a light `#e5e7eb` hairline in a dark theme. Measured in the browser, not reasoned about: `rgb(229, 231, 235)` before, `rgb(42, 42, 49)` after. The settings page had seven of the same fault, six of them panels whose `bg-surface-lighter/50` computed to fully transparent.
- **Stopped the probe leaving residue, then proved the residue cannot come back.** The cleanup ran *after* the assertions with no `finally`, so one thrown error left a service on the board permanently — which is exactly how five of them accumulated. It is now in a `finally`, and the "cleaned up after itself" assertion runs there too, so a probe that dies still tidies and still reports. A new phase covers the naming rule: a post about another product must read as clear for this service and raise nothing.
- **Verified end to end with the probe running under the exact conditions that caused the fault.** With the API pointed at the stub that answers every query, the service the post names raised its notice and the other thirteen services raised nothing across ~50 minutes of sweeps — the same window that previously produced 149 alerts. `probe-outage-board` finishes **36/36**, and afterwards the database holds exactly one alert. The page itself was read back through CDP: one alert card, zero empty states, dividers on the theme token, no console errors and no failed requests.

**Decisions worth remembering**
- **The screenshot's least obvious defect was the most expensive one.** The mismatched body looked like a cosmetic confusion; it was the whole board quoting one stranger's post. The tell was that the same text appeared on five unrelated services.
- **Delete the fabrication, then recapture the seed.** Cleaning the database alone would have looked fixed and been one `db:seed-from-snapshots` away from returning.
- **A probe's cleanup belongs in a `finally`, and its assertion belongs with it.** "The probe cleaned up after itself" asserted from *inside* the cleanup path is worth more than the same line at the end of a happy run.
- **The opacity-modifier trap bit again, in the same file family.** `bg-surface-lighter/40` on the installer card this morning, `border-surface-border/60` and `bg-surface-lighter/50` here. It never errors; the element just falls back. Read computed styles, never the class attribute.
- **A failed assertion is not always the product failing.** The one red line in the first probe run was my own regex: I checked for `name` in a detail that says `naming`. Fixed the assertion, not the product, and re-ran to 36/36.

**Notes for next time**
- **Reported, not fixed: `runAlertCheck` has no in-flight guard.** It is called by `POST /service-alerts/refresh` and by a 20-second timer plus a five-minute interval, and a sweep takes minutes on a host without egress — so a manual refresh lands mid-sweep routinely, and the probe's dozen refreshes guarantee it. The counters and the clear-streak map are module-level, so overlapping sweeps share them. Nothing observable went wrong in ~50 minutes of deliberate overlap, and the probe passes 36/36 under it, so I did not change it: proving harm needs its own test, and a lock is not a one-line change. Worth doing before the poll interval is shortened.
- **The white/rose left border on an informational card is the theme, not a severity mistake**: the active palette maps `cyber` to red, so `!border-l-cyber-500` reads as red. Check the palette before calling a colour wrong.
- **Auto-sync swept this work into two of its own commits** (`ee45e14`, `2d80b92`) while it was in progress, message and all. Nothing was lost, but the record for this prompt lives here rather than in the commit log.
- **This host has no internet egress**, so a monitor sweep takes ~4 minutes and `probe-outage-board` needs ~50. It is worth knowing before concluding a refresh has hung.

### Prompt 239 — The Uptime Monitors page explains itself
**Timestamp:** 2026-10-07 | **Status:** ✅ Completed | **Duration:** ~35 min
**BuildNotes IDs:** 2026.10.7.041 - The Uptime Monitors page explains what its three checks do, and why you would add one

> Write a better description of what this is for on the page. Explain what the Uptime monitors do and howan example of usage would look like. Please it in the page under the Uptime Monitors header

**What I did**
- **Wrote the description from the monitor's own code rather than from the form.** `observeMonitor` is the spec: a website check compares the status code against `expectStatus` (200) and calls anything else an outage; an SSL check reads the certificate's `valid_to`, raises an **informational** notice within `sslWarnDays` (30) and an **outage** once it has expired; a DNS check resolves the hostname and calls a failure an outage. Each kind is described by the failure it catches, because that is the part nobody can infer from a dropdown that says "Website / SSL expiry / DNS".
- **Made the example the same shape as the form.** Three rows using the page's own columns — name, kind, target — so the example reads as something you could type in: a website check for the portal answering with an error page, an SSL check for the certificate that expires over a weekend, a DNS check for mail stopping when the name stops resolving. A client portal going dark in three ways is the argument for the page existing.
- **Checked the example against the code before writing it, which caught a wrong one.** The DNS branch calls `new URL(monitorUrl)` and resolves `u.hostname`, so a bare `mail.client.com` throws and reports a bogus outage — the target has to be a URL even for a DNS check. The example uses `https://mail.client.com` and the copy says the host is what is read, so the path is ignored.
- **Added the two things that otherwise make the page look broken to a first-time user**: nothing runs until **Uptime monitors** is switched on in Configuration, and targets must be reachable from the internet because the checks go through the same egress policy as everything else — a private or link-local address is refused, and the refusal lands on the alert with its reason rather than passing silently.
- **Fixed the page's one-line description in the header, which was false.** `Layout.tsx` advertised "their own schedules, history and status"; the checks run on the shared five-minute Service Alerts tick, and this page shows neither history nor status. Now: "Website, SSL-expiry and DNS checks on targets you name: a failure raises a Service Alert."
- **Propagated the constraint to Help**, which had never stated it: the uptime-monitors walkthrough gains a note on the egress policy and on the path being ignored.

**Decisions worth remembering**
- **Match the page's idiom, not the design system, when the page predates the design system.** `Monitors.tsx` is inline-styled with raw hex and is on the lint's legacy allowlist; writing the new block in Tailwind tokens would have made the explanation look like it belonged to a different application. Same palette, same `style={{ }}` shape, and the token lint still passes with exactly its five known offenders.
- **A short description on a page is still a claim.** "Their own schedules, history and status" was three claims and none of them held. The new line says one thing the page can keep.
- **The example is documentation that has to run.** A worked example that would fail if typed in is worse than no example, which is why the DNS target is a URL.

**Notes for next time**
- **Worth fixing, not fixed here: the DNS check resolves only A records.** `dns.resolve4` on an IPv6-only hostname rejects, so a monitor on such a target reports an outage that is not real. Out of scope for a copy change, and it needs an assertion of its own.
- **The page is otherwise thin**: no edit, no delete, no last-checked column, no history, despite being one of the few places in the app where a person configures something that will page them. The copy now explains it; the page itself is still the plainest screen in the product.
- **Two headings say much the same thing** — the layout's page title and the page's own `<h1>`. Pre-existing, left alone.

### Prompt 240 — Alert Webhooks: the delivery that never happened, and a page that explains itself
**Timestamp:** 2026-10-07 | **Status:** ✅ Completed | **Duration:** ~2 h
**BuildNotes IDs:** 2026.10.7.042 - Alert Webhooks deliver for real, and the page explains every field

> Do the same thing for Alert Webhooks. Be more descriptive of what each field does. Redesign the page if necessary

**What I did**
- **Went looking for what to describe before writing a word of it, and found nothing to describe.** The page registers endpoints and lists deliveries, so I traced the deliveries back: `alertWebhookDelivery` is only ever *read* (by the log endpoint) and *seeded* (by sample data). There is no dispatcher — no POST to a registered URL, no signature, no retry, no attempt counting. Two schema fields had been waiting for it all along: `WebhookConfig.retryCount` (default 3) and a `pending` delivery status, neither reachable from any code path.
- **Also found the subscriptions were to events that do not exist.** A registration defaulted to `alert.opened` / `alert.resolved`; nothing in the application emits either. The real names are `service_alert.raised` / `service_alert.resolved` — the ones the sample data used and the monitor produces. So an endpoint registered from this page could not have received anything even with a dispatcher behind it.
- **Built the missing half rather than describing a feature that was not there.** `services/webhookDispatch.ts` fans events out to the active endpoints that asked for them: one signed POST per event, `X-C7-Signature` as HMAC-SHA256 over the exact body, retried up to that endpoint's own `retryCount` with a widening gap, and one delivery row per event recording status and attempts. The pending row is written before the first attempt, so the log shows work in flight and a crash leaves a visible pending row rather than silence.
- **Fire-and-forget, deliberately.** A webhook endpoint belongs to somebody else and may be slow or gone; the poll that raised the alert must not wait for it. Every send therefore runs detached from the caller, and the call sites in the monitor are `void emitWebhookEvent(...)` so a bad endpoint cannot delay an outage.
- **Routed it through `safeFetch` with the `webhook` purpose.** A user-supplied URL fetched server-side is the exact shape of an SSRF, and `safeFetch` already carries the address policy — including the check that a public name has not been pointed at 127.0.0.1. The registration form also validates the URL as literal text, so a typo is refused while the person is still looking at the field.
- **Gave the three fields that existed no meaning in the UI real ones**: events are now chosen at registration from the catalogue the dispatcher reads (a subscription to nothing is refused), `retryCount` is a field with a description and a 1–5 range, and the secret is handed over once with a copy button instead of being generated and thrown away.
- **Wrote the page for someone wiring a receiver at the other end.** It explains what a webhook is for here, what each field does, what every column of the log means, what each status means, and the exact request that arrives — method, the three headers, a sample body and a short Express handler that verifies the signature. **Send test** exists so a receiver can be proved without waiting for an incident; **Park** stops deliveries but keeps the history; **Remove** takes the history with it, because an endpoint that no longer exists cannot be fixed.
- **Probed the delivery contract rather than trusting it.** `probe-alert-webhooks.mjs` stands up a receiver and drives it: a raised alert arrives signed and is logged as delivered; an endpoint subscribed to the other event is not called; the resolved event reaches the endpoint that wanted it, with `resolvedAt`; a failing endpoint is attempted exactly `retryCount` times and logged as failed with that count; the test button sends one attempt and reports a 500 back to the page; a parked endpoint receives nothing while keeping its row; editing moves the address and keeps the secret; removing takes the deliveries with it. **45 passed, 0 failed.**
- **Acted on what the probe and the page then exposed in sample data.** The seeded endpoints point at `hooks.example.com`; while they were active every real alert produced three failed attempts against a host that does not resolve, so a fresh install would open the page on a wall of failures. They are seeded parked now, and the noise they had already produced was cleared.
- **Redesigned the page off the legacy allowlist.** `Webhooks.tsx` was hand-styled with raw hex; it is now the design system's components and tokens, which let me remove it from the design-token allowlist — the lint proves the rewrite has no raw hex left.

**Decisions worth remembering**
- **"Describe this page" turned out to be "this page describes something that does not happen".** Every field description I could have written about delivery would have been false, and the previous prompt in this session was itself a fix for a description that had drifted from the truth. Checking the feature before writing its copy is what made this a delivery pipeline instead of a paragraph.
- **Two unused schema fields are a design note from the original author.** `retryCount` and the `pending` status were the intended shape all along; using them meant the feature arrived looking like the data model rather than like something bolted on.
- **The subscription default was the quietest bug in the change.** Even with a dispatcher, `alert.opened` would have delivered nothing, and it would have looked like the endpoint's fault. A default that cannot fire is worse than no default.
- **A probe's own bugs are worth reading twice.** The first run failed 401 on every call because `signIn` returns `{ status, data }` and I read `.token` off the wrapper: a whole page of red that said nothing about the product.
- **Sample data has to survive the feature becoming real.** A fake endpoint was harmless while nothing sent anything; the moment delivery worked it turned into permanent failure noise. Seeding it parked is the fix that keeps the sample honest.

**Notes for next time**
- **Ticket events are still not wired.** `ticket.created` and `ticket.sla_breached` exist in the seeded sample data and in the integrations thinking, but nothing emits them yet; the page only offers what can actually be delivered, so a ticket subscription is not offered rather than offered and dead. Wiring them is the natural next slice — `POST /tickets` and wherever the SLA sweep runs.
- **`routes/bulk.ts` has a parallel webhook trio** (`GET/POST/DELETE /bulk/webhooks`) that is dead code per PLAN-018 A8, and it still writes `events: req.body.events || []` with no validation. It is unreachable from the UI; worth deleting rather than fixing.
- **The delivery log is capped at the most recent 100 rows** and has no pagination or filtering yet. Fine for a handful of endpoints; thin once someone is debugging a flapping integration.
- **The 15-minute auto-sync will likely sweep part of this into its own commit** while the records are being written; check `git log` before assuming a change is uncommitted.
